items.originalTitle: Havana, Caracas and Trump’s Unfinished Business in Latin America
items.author: Ian Bremmer
items.title: Havana, Caracas and Trump’s Unfinished Business in Latin America
items.summary: Pedestrians walk past a sign reading "No one surrenders here" in Havana, Cuba, Nov. 14, 2026. —Joaquin Hernandez-Xinhua-Getty Images “I want to get Cuba done before I leave you,” President Donald Trump told a conservative radio host on Nov. 12. It is a reminder that, despite the historic beating his party took in the midterm elections, Trump continues to see Latin America as a crucial part of his legacy. Though it was New York Post headline writers who coined the term “Donroe Doctrine,” a play on President James Monroe’s insistence two centuries ago that the United States alone would dominate the Americas, Trump has embraced the term as he thinks about his legacy. The President has plenty of unfinished business in the region—and the incoming opposition-dominated Congress will surely launch investigations into many parts of Trump’s Latin America agenda. Hearings on U.S. management of Venezuelan oil revenues , U.S. strikes targeting boats in international waters, and the use of El Salvador’s maximum-security prison for deportees are a virtual certainty. But Trump is more likely to defy Democratic lawmakers than to compromise with them, and, in truth, most of his policy priorities in the region can be pursued through executive actions, which can be undone by a successor but don’t require new legislation from Congress. He can attempt to use tariffs and other trade measures to pressure governments, administer the Venezuela sanctions and licensing framework, provide security assistance to allies in the region, and even order military action in Cuba, as he has threatened. In fact, the future of the Donroe Doctrine depends less on Congress than on the ambitions of his Secretary of State, Marco Rubio. Rubio may well leave government early to launch a run for president in 2028—but even if he decides to run, he is likely to keep his high-profile job into next year, giving him the chance to work on issues that matter most to him. This brings us back to Cuba. Rubio, the Florida-born son of Cuban immigrants, remains eager to bring lasting change to the island. At a campaign rally in October, Trump joked that “We’ll drop [Rubio] in the middle of Cuba , he’ll solve that problem in about two minutes…Cuba’s coming our way.” The president will back plans to force an economic deal on the impoverished island’s Communist Party leadership. Rubio will also want to set a firm timeline for multiparty elections in Venezuela, even if he leaves the administration for the campaign trail. Both the president and his top diplomat regard the arrest of former strongman Nicolás Maduro and the oil deals that Trump has struck with Maduro’s former loyalists, who remain in power in Caracas, as the administration’s greatest foreign policy success. But for the Secretary of State and his own political future, setting Venezuela on a path toward democracy will be especially important. He is also likely to push for talks to restructure Venezuela’s foreign debt to help stabilize the country’s struggling economy. And what about the rest of the region? Trump will continue to aggressively use the threat of tariffs to force President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico to maintain her country’s cooperation in preventing Central American migrant caravans from reaching the U.S. southern border. On Nov. 12, Trump threatened that tariffs would be “ IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED ” if her commitment wavered. In Brazil, the recent presidential election didn’t turn out as the White House hoped, but Trump has indicated he’ll work with the re-elected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on shared priorities. The region’s more Trump-friendly governments hope to make the most of his remaining time in office. The White House will continue to provide financial and security assistance to Argentina’s Javier Milei, Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa and Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella. Yet leaders across the region, whatever their relationship with Trump, expect to outlast him in office. They know that the next American president—Republican or Democrat—might well be someone far less interested in Latin America, and that all they can be sure of is that the U.S. role in the hemisphere may shift once again.

items.originalTitle: 2028 Democrats say Nvidia news is another example of corruption in government
items.author: Jason Beeferman and Sam Sutton
items.title: 2028 Democrats say Nvidia news is another example of corruption in government
items.summary: Democrats weighing 2028 presidential bids are using Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as another opportunity to accuse the White House of corruption. It’s a message that appeared to work well for them earlier this month: Voters resoundingly rejected President Donald Trump’s agenda, angry over high prices and an economy that benefited a select few. Now, Democrats are keen to repeat that core political argument — especially after Trump took credit for helping reinstate Huang. “This is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said in a statement . “The sheer corruption and weakness of Donald Trump is hurting America and putting our economy and national security at risk,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro wrote in a statement , describing Huang’s reinstatement is an example of “a rigged system that protects those at the very top.” Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel told Decoded by POLITICO: “The number one rule is that the rule of law will hold the banker, the billionaire, and the baker to the same standard,” he said. “Now you tell me: What’s good about capitalism when you have a president of the United States pressing a public board to reverse themselves on their own governance? What is good about that decision?” Pritzker, Shapiro and Emanuel are among the wide field of prospective Democratic presidential candidates. Their immediate decision to criticize Huang’s return as head of the massive chip company puts them at odds with top Silicon Valley leaders , including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to be reinstated after he stepped down. The public statements also show that these top Democrats are holding onto the playbook that campaigns used to dominate in the midterm elections, when the party firmly regained control of the House, Senate and statehouses around the country. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and two company employees . On Monday, he was reinstated by a unanimous board vote after Trump publicly called for his return and pushed for it with board members over the weekend. Huang’s close relationship with Trump has come under scrutiny since news of his affairs broke. The two spoke frequently, with Trump even calling Huang directly while he was on stage at a tech conference. The New York Times previously reported that Trump and top administration officials were aware that Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy — but chose not to act. And Trump critics from both parties have pointed to Nvidia’s $25 million donation to the president’s White House ballroom project under Huang’s leadership as an example of Trump’s alleged corruption. In a statement, the White House said that “today’s decision by Nvidia will preserve America’s technological edge over China, strengthen our national security, and ensure the future of SI continues to be built in America.” “The Huang situation at its core is about corruption,” Republican former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who is considering another presidential bid , said last week, referencing the ballroom donation. “So when something came up that was serious, what happened? Trump walked away from it and wouldn’t deal with it. That’s the intersection of corruption and incompetence that causes the American people to lose.” Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who also is considering a bid, told Axios the move from Huang amounted to a double standard for Trump’s allies and the rest of America. "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee,” he said. “You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate where, frankly, if that was any of us we would be held to a different type of standard.” That messaging could continue to prove effective. During the midterms, Democratic groups zeroed in on corruption in the White House and sought to connect high gas and grocery prices to a Trump administration they said flouted basic ethical rules while protecting and enriching powerful allies of the president. They connected corruption to the Epstein files, data centers , stock trading and other topics, reinforcing that unscrupulous dealings were at play while costs were going up. Polling obtained by POLITICO in the weeks leading up to Election Day shows the vast majority of Americans — both Democrats and Republicans — say corruption is driving up their costs. And a September poll from Gallup also found about 90 percent of Americans believe corruption is rampant in government. Democrats and several Republicans on Capitol Hill are pushing for more transparency on the extent to which Nvidia’s chips ended up in Chinese hands and further details on Huang’s relationship with suspected spy Alice Huang. “Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy,” Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is running to lead Senate Democrats, said in a briefing to reporters. Van Hollen was speculated as a possible 2028 presidential candidate, though he’s now ruled out a White House bid. “We know that President Trump owns Nvidia stock. We know that Jensen Huang contributed to the inauguration, attended a million-dollar plate at Mar-a-Lago and essentially Jensen Huang has been running the Trump administration's AI and big tech policy,” Van Hollen added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Immigration Is Not a Fringe Issue
items.author: Greisa Martínez Rosas
items.title: Immigration Is Not a Fringe Issue
items.summary: —Maria Kraynova—Getty Images At a Senate forum on ICE violence, I listened to the sons of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo describe the morning their father was shot dead by ICE agents while on his way to work. Besides them sat and wept the families of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti . Next to me were clergy wearing t-shirts that said “ Connected Americans ” and whispering prayers as they listened to the testimony of families whose loved ones had been killed in the streets. While a number of elected officials sat in the front of the room, they were not the center. The families and those of us there to bear witness were. The demands made that day by people like Lorenzo’s sons were not unfamiliar to me. They’re the demands I hear from people every day: swift justice that remedies what our communities have been forced to endure and a future where all working people can live with safety, stability, and dignity. It takes courage to speak out when your voice breaks. These families did it anyway. Meanwhile, throughout the midterms, Democratic candidates were advised by centrist think tanks and commentators to talk less about immigration and more about the economy. As if one were a political liability and the other a path back to working families. No one in that Senate room was living a separate problem. The failure of both Democrats and Republicans to deliver a path to citizenship has pushed economic security further out of reach for working people, leaving millions of workers vulnerable to deportation, family separation, and a future defined by instability and uncertainty. Multiply that across every workplace where someone has been killed, detained, deported, or stripped of their ability to work, and the consequences are anything but abstract. They affect us all. Immigrants sustain the industries, workplaces, and communities we all depend on. And those who insist we must choose between a path to citizenship or supporting working families have yet to stand with the families bearing the cost of that false choice. The midterm results should make it impossible to ignore the truth: there is no such thing as a functioning economy for working people without immigrants. Voters rejected an administration whose immigration policies have made life more expensive and less secure for working families. Even the President admitted what those families already knew. In an interview with 60 Minutes , Donald Trump said that his mass deportations “might have been too tough,” costing both him and Republicans control of Congress. “I get hurt because we also took people who had good jobs.” Soon after the episode aired, Trump named Stephen Miller, the central architect of the deadly raids, family separations, and mass deportations , as his next White House Chief of Staff. A president who acknowledges the cost of mass deportations went on to promote the man who built it. This is a warning to every member of the incoming Congress, newly elected and returning: the election did not end this fight. It's likely they will escalate it. We will be organizing so that Members of Congress defend the people they were elected to represent. What Americans are up against is formidable. The numbers describe the mass deportation machinery Congress has helped fund. ICE's detention population grew by more than 70% between January 2025 and April 2026. Congress still approved approximately $75 billion in additional ICE funding, including $45 billion for immigration detention, despite polling showing that 58% of Americans believe ICE's enforcement actions have gone too far. And in the last two years, 60 people have died in immigration enforcement custody or encounters, according to The Guardian . The harm does not stop with immigrants. An investigation by ProPublica revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in immigration enforcement practices. Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti amongst them. Our broken, violent immigration system impacts neighborhoods, workplaces, and families across the country. No one is left out of its reach. And our economy suffers when the millions of working people whose labor helps sustain it are left vulnerable without a path to citizenship. My home state of Texas shows what it looks like when a candidate refuses to treat immigration, human rights, and the economy as separate issues. Salgado Araujo lived and worked in Texas for 35 years, putting his three sons through college as a proud, hardworking father. As James Talarico campaigned for his Senate seat, he spoke of his death and committed to ICE accountability and citizenship. Four months to the day after the shooting, the now senator-elect visited Salgado’s memorial in Houston, pledging to seek justice and adding his “I voted” sticker, alongside many other fellow Texans, to the memorial site where Salgado Araujo was shot and killed. The sticker can be seen as a promise; an oath to use every tool available to protect communities against the terror that has stolen the lives of fathers, mothers, workers, and loved ones across our communities. The organizers, voters, community leaders, and ordinary Americans who made it possible for Talarico to win are now watching whether he and other newly-elected Members of Congress will honor that oath in January. Strongly worded letters, congressional investigations, and modest cuts to immigration enforcement funding will not be enough in this new Congress. Democrats must pursue a fundamental change in direction, starting with a pathway to citizenship and ensuring immigrants are protected in every legislative priority the new Congress advances. Voters want leaders willing to confront an enforcement agenda that is tearing families apart, destabilizing workplaces, and wasting billions of their taxpayer dollars, while they’re left struggling simply to make ends meet. And they want leaders who understand that protecting immigrant workers is essential to building an economy that works for everyone. Electoral wins alone will not protect the millions of people—both citizens and immigrants—whose livelihoods and futures remain at risk. We cannot afford another Congress that recognizes the issue but fails to deliver a solution. Voters, especially Black, Latino, young, and working-class people, have done their part by rejecting Trump’s agenda at the ballot box. Now Democrats must do theirs. With Stephen Miller's ability to escalate the administration's cruelty, the incoming Congress cannot settle for symbolic resistance or half measures. A pathway to citizenship is the floor of what Congress must deliver. Millions of working people will be organizing to make it so, because the people we love belong here for good.

items.originalTitle: Measles Is Back in the U.S. What Happens Next?
items.author: Alice Park
items.title: Measles Is Back in the U.S. What Happens Next?
items.summary: A child receives the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella in Lubbock, Texas in 2025. —Jan Sonnenmair/Stringer—Getty Images On Nov. 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declared that measles is no longer considered "eliminated" in the U.S. In the past year, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded more than 5,800 cases of measles—the highest caseload since 1991. Vaccination programs and increased monitoring of incoming measles cases helped the U.S. to eliminate measles in 2000, meaning there was no consistent spread of the virus within the country for more than a year. Since then, sporadic cases of the virus have been reported—but from people who had traveled to other parts of the world where the disease is endemic. No longer. So far, the CDC reports that 47 states have reported at least one case of measles, and wastewater reports of cases of the virus have increased in recent months. “What makes this different from pop-up cases that we expect year to year is that we failed to interrupt the chain of transmission of the virus,” says Steph Batalis, research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. “That’s a big deal. We have tools to do that, yet we failed to do so. That should raise serious questions about the conditions that allowed that to happen.” Days after the announcement, Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that HHS will "work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.” While Kennedy went on to blame COVID for interrupting childhood vaccinations, public-health officials point to several other more recent actions that Kennedy, a long-time skeptic of vaccines, has taken that may have also contributed to the rise of measles cases in the U.S. In 2025, Kennedy dismissed the CDC’s Advisory Committee for Immunization Practices, an independent group of experts that sets vaccine recommendations for the U.S. that state health departments and professional organizations generally follow, and replaced the committee with members who shared his vaccine skepticism. HHS also attempted to revise the childhood immunization schedule, removing recommendations for most children to receive annual flu and COVID shots , and emphasizing shared-decision making about vaccines between families and physicians. Professional health organizations—including the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Physicians, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America—sued HHS over these changes. A court suspended the new ACIP from continuing to meet and reverted the childhood immunization schedule back to its original recommendations. Such confusion around vaccines has likely played a significant role in the U.S. measles outbreaks of the past year, says Dr. Jon Andrus, professor of global health at the Milken Institute School of Public Health at George Washington University. “Any successful public-health program requires excellence in scientific and operational strategies about how you are vaccinating, when you vaccinate them, and what vaccines you use, all based on evidence,” he says. “And none of that works without political commitment. If that is undermined, and if the messages coming from the highest level sows seeds of doubt, then you have people doubting the strategies and not vaccinating their child.” He and other public-health experts say that the loss of the measles elimination status isn’t merely a symbolic change. It’s a warning sign of a weakened public-health system fueled by deteriorating trust in scientific experts and mixed messages from health leaders who the public normally turn to for advice. And the change in the U.S.’s status may have deeper consequences for public health, beyond just more cases of measles. Here's what's worrying experts. There are long-term consequences of getting measles Some of the public’s attitudes about vaccines—including the one for measles, which is part of the MMR series—center around unsubstantiated claims that the vaccines contain toxic chemicals that do more harm than good, and that the measles shot in particular is linked to a higher risk of autism, a claim that has for years been scientifically debunked. Because measles has not been common in the U.S. for decades, a generation of parents and doctors have not seen how devastating the disease can be. “Measles in Latin means ‘miserable,’” says Andrus. Having measles can cause pneumonia, ear infections, and encephalitis, or brain swelling. But even if a child recovers from a measles infection, the disease may affect his or her health for years to come. “Measles infections can contribute to deafness, blindness, and, depending on the neurological insult, intellectual and physical disability as well,” says Dr. Micah Niermann, an internal medicine and pediatric physician at Gillette Children’s in St. Paul, Minn. “Some may need lifelong care, and their lives and the lives of their families are altered permanently.” More recently, scientists have also uncovered another way the virus can impact a person’s health, even if they recover from the infection. “The measles virus can attack immune cells and make them less effective for some prolonged period of time,” says Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “We don’t know how long, but for that period after measles, the child is more susceptible to other kinds of infections that they are ordinarily immune to.” The measles virus has the ability to wipe out whatever memory the immune cells have accumulated to recognize other pathogens—including those introduced by vaccines. “A child who has had measles is at risk of suffering from or dying from other vaccine-preventable diseases, and that risk goes out three years or longer,” says Andrus. There is also a rare but still meaningful risk of longer term consequences of measles known as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a condition caused by the measles virus destroying brain cells. SSPE’s symptoms can start years after a measles infection but cannot be triggered by the measles vaccine. Children may start to show changes in personality and experience seizures or involuntary movements of their arms and legs, which then leads to dementia and problems eating, swallowing, and breathing. The condition is almost always fatal. Children under two who get measles are at higher risk of developing SPPE later in life, and the best way to prevent the condition is to protect those children from getting measles in the first place with the vaccine, or for those too young to be vaccinated, to ensure those around them are vaccinated so they are less likely to get exposed to measles. Some people may need a booster shot Most adults who have received two doses of the MMR vaccine do not need to get a booster; the two doses provide 97% protection against infection for a lifetime, according to the CDC . Most people who were born before 1957 also don’t need an additional shot since they were likely exposed to measles because there was no vaccine yet available. The only groups that may need to consider a booster are people who might not know if they received two doses of the vaccine or people who are immunocompromised, such as those undergoing chemotherapy. They might benefit from the booster after, but not while, they are undergoing chemotherapy, to give their immune systems additional support. “Say you are undergoing a bone marrow transplant or chemotherapy: this adds another element of risk assessment for patients,” says Niermann. “There are people at risk who could get ill from measles.” Another group of people who should consider a booster are those born from 1963 to 1967. In that time, an old version of the vaccine was used that might not be as effective as the current version, which relies on a weakened, live version of the measles virus. People who are currently 59-63 should discuss with their health care provider whether they need a booster. Outbreaks won't stop at measles “Measles is the canary in the coal mine,” says Racine. “This is not just about measles. The reason we’re seeing measles first is that it’s more contagious than any other infectious disease." If one person is infected, for instance, 90% of people in close contact with that person can get infected as well. And the virus can stay airborne from an infected person’s cough or sneeze for up to two hours. "It’s as if measles is knocking on the door of every household in the country saying, ‘Guess what, I’m here. I’m back,'" Racine says. "'You may have thought I got lost and went someplace else. I’m here to tell you that you forgot to lock the door, and I’m coming in. And not only that, but I’m not by myself. Take a look behind me, I’ve brought a bunch of friends: influenza, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae, pertussis, whooping cough. Look down the list, and you see polio back there too. They’re coming—we’re all coming.’” Measles is so contagious that it’s often the first outbreak public-health experts see as childhood vaccination rates decline. “We often say that measles outbreaks are a signal of a weaker immunization system,” says Dr. William Moss, professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “This is a red flag and tells us we’re not doing what we need to be doing to control measles.” As vaccination rates fall in general, other vaccine-preventable diseases will start to spike. “I will be surprised if we don’t start to see more cases of congenital rubella and mumps,” says Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America and head of the division of infectious diseases at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine. Measles outbreaks could threaten U.S. biosecurity The measles outbreak may also affect the U.S.’s ability to protect itself from infectious threats. The health care costs associated with measles—in terms of immediate care and the potential longer terms consequences if they develop SPPE—are already burdening overstretched local and state health resources. Doctors and public-health experts who could be dedicated to focusing on other threats are now required to manage preventable illnesses. “Public-health departments are on the front lines, and if they are addressing measles outbreaks, which is something that is avoidable, then there are opportunity costs for how they are able to address other issues,” says Niermann. Even more concerning, says Batalis, are the mixed messages coming from federal health authorities . “If people are looking to get [health] information for themselves, the question becomes: Who is filling that vacuum of information?” she says. “If it’s not filled by trustworthy sources and if the government is discrediting trustworthy sources, then who fills the gap? Now we’re seeing reports that a lot of vaccine disinformation is coming from bots, which raises a lot of questions about how that makes us more vulnerable, and how could adversaries exploit that. There is a security consideration in addition to public health.” How can the U.S. regain its status as having eliminated measles? “The very first thing that needs to happen is a recognition that an error has been made,” says Racine. “And unfortunately, in the condition that we’re currently in, the folks who are in charge of this have not been willing or able to recognize that a mistake has been made here. Until that happens, we are not able to have the full force of all the government authorities—from local, state, and national levels—working in conjunction with pediatricians and the community and public-health officials to seriously address what is going on.” While CDC director Erica Schwartz has said that the CDC is deploying resources to areas experiencing measles outbreaks, Racine says those cases will continue to spread if there isn’t a stronger and more unified message about the best way to control measles: by supporting vaccination and reiterating that it is safe. While both Kennedy and Schwartz have said they support measles vaccines, Kennedy has also stated that protection from the vaccine “waned quickly” and that the shot has not been “safely tested”—positions not supported by scientific evidence. “There are going to be long-term consequence of what is happening today,” says Racine.

items.originalTitle: This Moderate Democrat Thinks Trump Could Help Rein In ICE
items.author: Philip Wang
items.title: This Moderate Democrat Thinks Trump Could Help Rein In ICE
items.summary: U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, poses for a photo at the Starr County Courthouse Annex Building on October 2, 2026 in Rio Grande City, Texas. —Gabriel V. Cárdenas–The Washington Post via Getty Images Representative Henry Cuellar has been in Congress for more than 20 years, representing a South Texas district that includes a big chunk of Texas' border with Mexico. Over the years, he has fended off pressures from both parties: Democrats have tried and failed to replace him with someone more liberal; Republicans have tried and failed to convince him to join the GOP. Now he's about to start a new term as part of the largest Democratic majority this century. While many of his colleagues want to battle the Trump Administration to rein in ICE, Cuellar sees things differently. He thinks Washington may be on the verge of the perfect conditions to finally fix the country's immigration system for good. “I told my Republican friends, the last time we had real immigration reform was [when] President Reagan was a Republican, and the House was controlled by Democrats," Cuellar tells TIME. "That's how you get the work done. It's got to be bipartisan.” Cuellar says discussions are already underway behind the scenes on how to work with the White House to actually pass immigration reform, something Congress has repeatedly tried and failed to accomplish for decades. He points to Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, and Reps. Sylvia Garcia and Rep. Veronica Escobar, both from Texas, as other Democrats who are helping craft language for the measures. “A good number” of congressional Republicans willing to talk seriously about immigration reform are also involved in the discussions, he says. Cuellar is set to chair the House subcommittee that oversees funding for the Department of Homeland Security. At the top of Cuellar’s wish list: put new guardrails on Immigration and Customs Enforcement, redirect billions of unspent funding allocated to immigration enforcement in the One Big Beautiful Bill, and streamline the visa process for millions of immigrant guest-workers. “If the president is the one that calls the decisions, we will reach an agreement,” the Texas Democrat says. Trump’s mixed signals Cuellar’s optimism on immigration reform stems in part from how Trump softened his tone on immigration right after the election. During a “60 Minutes” interview, Trump acknowledged that some of the immigration policies pushed by hardline Republicans were “too tough” and that he was open to a pathway to permanent residency for undocumented immigrants who have been staying in the U.S. for more than a decade. But around the same time, Trump also promoted Stephen Miller as the White House Chief of Staff, elevating the architect of the mass deportation agenda to the most powerful unelected position in Washington. Any potential immigration deal is further complicated by Cuellar and Trump’s unusual history. In 2025, President Trump pardoned Cuellar and his wife after both were indicted for accepting thousands of dollars from the Azerbaijan government and a Mexican commercial bank. Following his pardon, Cuellar continued to run and won his reelection as a Democrat, which enraged Trump who expected Cuellar to switch parties. Last month, Trump slammed Cuellar in a Truth Social post, calling him “disloyal” and “ungrateful.” While Cuellar saw signs of hope from Trump’s comments on “60 Minutes,” other Democratic lawmakers and some immigration policy experts were far more skeptical . Trump, after all, is behind the federal government’s most aggressive immigration enforcement operation in decades. Read more: An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates Trump’s comments also drew pushback from his closest allies, who interpreted the President’s comments as amnesty. Vice President JD Vance on Thursday criticized the idea of offering a legal pathway to undocumented immigrants, saying that any effort to “give amnesty to people who have broken our laws” is “morally and electorally disastrous.” But none of those comments dented Cuellar’s excitement. “Other people are hardliners, but the President, I feel, will be willing to make an agreement,” Cuellar insists. Jorge Loweree, the managing director of programs at the American Immigration Council, says that Trump has long floated the idea of offering undocumented immigrants a legal pathway to stay in the country, but previous efforts among congressional Republicans during Trump’s first term failed due to the GOP’s internal divisions. Trump has never been given an opportunity to sign or veto an immigration bill at the White House. “If Congress managed to get it [a legalization bill] through both chambers and send it to the President and call his bluff, it's not clear what he would do,” Loweree says. TIME has reached out to the White House for comments. The power of the purse Instead of passing a standalone bill, Democrats may find it easier to reshape the immigration system through the budget process. Cuellar is set to chair the House subcommittee that oversees funding for the Department of Homeland Security. An American Immigration Council analysis estimates that ICE had roughly $91 billion remaining from two Republican reconciliation laws as of October, with another $45.6 billion available to Customs and Border Protection—guaranteeing both agencies the ability to carry out mass deportation operations for years without congressional oversight. Last week, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries reiterated his interest in redirecting ICE funding. “We believe that taxpayer dollars should actually be spent to make life affordable for the American people, not to brutalize or kill American citizens, or law-abiding immigrants,” Jeffries said during a press conference. Democrats in both chambers have previously introduced bills either redirecting tens of billions of dollars to fund Medicaid or clawing back the funding altogether. Cuellar suggested that legislators are looking into whether that money could be redirected to other agencies inside DHS that have been impacted by the layoffs implemented by DOGE last year. “Can it be moved from ICE into other items? You've got FEMA. You've got other agencies that certainly could use more assistance. We are looking at all the legalities as to what is possible and what is not,” he explains. Detention centers and border security Cuellar’s congressional district in South Texas is home to three ICE detention centers. He has also examined the conditions inside Dilley, the country’s largest family immigration detention facility, which is in Texas but not in his district, and has drawn a string of accusations of medical neglect . And he’s been watching how ICE has been buying up properties around the country to drastically expand its network of detention facilities. The agency overpaid by at least 50% for nine of the 11 warehouses that it had intended to convert to detention centers, but is now trying to offload, according to a recent report from the Government Accountability Office. The report also estimated that ICE pays more than $13 million a month for detention beds that sit empty. All of that is shaping his approach to trying to overhaul ICE, as is a ticking clock. There is likely little time to rein in ICE’s spending on detention centers before the agency signs more contracts with private prison companies. The One Big Beautiful Bill signed by Trump in 2025 granted ICE $45 billion for immigration detention centers and made the funds available through the 2029 fiscal year. The GAO report found that ICE’s current plans indicate that the agency expects to obligate the remaining detention funds by the end of the 2027 fiscal year. Cuellar has a history of being a staunch supporter of border security. In January, he was one of just seven House Democrats to join Republicans in voting for an ICE funding bill. Among the broader party, support for pairing ICE reform with border security has been gaining more traction among Democrats since the end of the Biden administration. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990, said in a Fox News interview on Thursday that she wants to see the federal government shore up funds for border security. “Texas has spent $20 billion on border security,” she says. “It is the responsibility of the federal government to keep our borders intact and secure, and Texas taxpayers should not be footing that bill to such an extent.” Cuellar sees that growing sentiment within his party as key to the next Congress finding a way to make sweeping changes to immigration that Trump could support. “Every immigration reform or full comprehensive immigration reform will have border security,” Cuellar says.

items.originalTitle: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
items.author: Jonathan Jones
items.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
items.summary: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London?

items.originalTitle: You Can See Everything in Elizabeth Holmes’s unblinking eyes. Or can you? | Jason Okundaye
items.author: Jason Okundaye
items.title: You Can See Everything in Elizabeth Holmes’s unblinking eyes. Or can you? | Jason Okundaye
items.summary: The idea that seeing is believing is turned on its head in this documentary about the inscrutable Theranos founder, a world-class liar who may just be completely unreadable Elizabeth Holmes doesn’t believe that she’s ever told a lie. She “knows” that she hasn’t committed any crime. And she has no reason to deceive you. While speaking, she is gazing at her interviewer, Nathan Fielder, with those enormous, blue, vacant, unsettling, unblinking eyes. She doesn’t break eye contact. This is You Can See Everything, Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, which, at her invitation, follows Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at their home in San Diego in the weeks up to her surrender to custody at federal prison. Holmes is the disgraced tech ex-billionaire whose startup Theranos claimed the ability to run hundreds of comprehensive blood tests from a single pinprick of blood. This false claim posed “immediate jeopardy” to the health of thousands of patients and defrauded investors of more than $700m.

items.summary: In 2026, the earth was rocked by more extreme weather and the moon seemed once again within our reach. The streets of our cities were rushed by celebrating sports fans and thronged with angry citizens. Technological change, with all the fear and excitement it brings, seemed to accelerate faster than ever. People reached for greatness —or, in a time of global conflict , simply for peace. We know all this because, despite everything that changes, we can still believe our own eyes. The essence of TIME's Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them. Inside the person viewing the image, a different, more mysterious process takes place. Something else clicks—at, say, the juxtaposition of a day at the beach and the smoke of a wildfire across the water. At the tension of high school students huddled on one side of a Paris bank building the moment riot police begin their charge on the other. Or, in Washington, D.C., on the 250th birthday of America, at far-right demonstrators masked in white sharing a subway car with a lone Black woman. Even when they appear to be special effects—from dogs that seem to disappear to an electrical storm phenomenon lighting up the sky above an ancient stone town—the resulting pictures capture a truth. These moments, and the others seen here, are the real deal. — Karl Vick Palestinian players for the Al-Ahly Club warm up before a match against Gaza Sports Club at a newly constructed field surrounded by buildings destroyed in Israeli ground and air operations, in Gaza City on Feb. 14. The Palestinian Football Federation created the field by clearing rubble and laying used artificial turf, providing a place for local teams and amputee players to return to the sport. Gaza’s main soccer stadium had been leveled during the Israel-Hamas war and was serving as a tent camp for displaced families. —Jehad Alshrafi—AP Photo Local residents and visitors relax on a beach on the edge of Odessa, Ukraine, as smoke from a fire rises in the background following a Russian missile strike during an air raid alert, on July 29. —Kostiantyn Liberov—Libkos/Getty Images A protester is handcuffed on snow-covered Nicollet Avenue in south Minneapolis on Jan. 24. Earlier that day, roughly a block away, federal agents had shot and killed Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse. Around 3000 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents were deployed to the region between Dec. 4th, 2025, and Feb. 12, 2026, in what at the time was described by the Department of Homeland Security as its largest immigration enforcement operation. —David Guttenfelder—The New York Times/Redux A man who had been detained by ICE is embraced upon his release from Delaney Hall Detention Facility in Newark, N.J., on May 27. The 1,000-bed facility, owned and operated by a private prison company, reopened for immigration detention in May 2025 amid the Trump Administration’s expanded deportation push. —Mark Peterson—Redux New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his wife, artist Rama Duwaji, celebrate his inauguration in Lower Manhattan on Jan. 1. Tens of thousands of New Yorkers braved freezing temperatures for a block party near City Hall marking the start of his administration. —Jutharat Pinyodoonyachet One of the first images captured during Artemis II’s seven-hour lunar flyby on April 6 reveals regions of the far side of the moon. The test flight carried NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen around the moon. The dark portion of Earth is experiencing nighttime. On Earth’s day side, swirling clouds are visible over the Australia and Oceania region. —NASA Birds flying among the Bison in front of the Grand Tetons, Wyoming, Nov 7. —Isaac Spotts Detainees, including children, wave signs during a demonstration at the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas, on Jan. 24. The protest followed the transfer of 5-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos and his father to the facility; detainees chanted “Libertad” — “Freedom.” —Brenda Bazán—AP A regional train passes a railroad crossing between flooded fields in Nidderau-Eichen near Frankfurt, Germany, on Feb. 18. —Michael Probst—AP Underground at South32’s Hermosa project in Arizona’s Patagonia Mountains, July 16. The zinc and manganese development was the first mining project accepted into FAST-41, a federal program designed to streamline environmental reviews and permitting for major infrastructure projects. The underground nature of the project minimizes its visible footprint. “We will mine for up to 70 years at this site, and only disturb 750 acres in total,” says Pat Risner, the project’s president. But nearby residents fear the project could contaminate the groundwater they depend on and damage habitat for wildlife, including jaguars and Mexican spotted owls. —Matt Black for TIME Workers install a large chandelier at a wedding hall in Kabul, Afghanistan, on July 21. The Taliban returned to power five years ago, in what they call the "liberation" of Afghanistan—which, for millions of Afghans, means anything but. —Tomas Munita—The New York Times/Redux Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro appears in a photograph posted by U.S. President Donald Trump on Truth Social on Jan. 3, following Maduro’s capture by U.S. forces. Trump identified the setting as the USS Iwo Jima, an amphibious assault ship in the Caribbean Sea. The raid marked the most direct U.S. intervention in Latin America since the 1989 invasion of Panama, which ousted its leader, Manuel Noriega. —@realDonaldTrump—Handout via Reuters A commuter sits surrounded by masked members of the far-right nationalist group Patriot Front, on a Metro train in Washington, D.C., on July 4, 2026, the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence. —Cheney Orr—Reuters A young boy dressed as an astronaut cheers beside a woman waving a flag during a watch party for the Artemis II crew’s return to Earth at the San Diego Air and Space Museum on April 10. The four astronauts’ splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off California marked the completion of NASA’s crewed test flight around the moon—the first such mission in more than 50 years. —Apu Gomes—AFP/Getty Images A coastal brown bear leaps into a river teeming with spawning sockeye salmon in Katmai National Park, Alaska, on Aug. 6. These salmon have traveled from Bristol Bay and the northern Pacific Ocean, swimming 100 miles inland up the freshwater Alagnak River to spawn and die in the exact gravel beds where they were born. The returning fish serve as the primary food source for bears preparing for winter hibernation, while their carcasses release vital marine nutrients that sustain the entire Alaskan tundra ecosystem. —Mike Rigney Enzo Fernandez #24 of Argentina fouls Pau Cubarsi #22 of Spain during the FIFA World Cup 2026 Final match between Spain and Argentina at New York New Jersey Stadium on July 19 in East Rutherford, N.J. —Al Bello—Getty Images Former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino smiles from the stage as demonstrators interrupt remarks he was giving at Rutgers University’s Douglass Student Center in New Brunswick, N.J., at a Nov. 16 talk hosted by the Rutgers Republicans. The fleeting electrical discharge formed high above thunderstorms near Barcelona, more than 500 kilometers away. Photographer Florian Riou spent days tracking the storms and calculating his vantage point; “I captured the shot I had been dreaming of,” he says. Sprites occur roughly 50 to 90 km above Earth’s surface, their vivid red glow produced by nitrogen molecules in the upper atmosphere. —Florian Riou A trick rider guides a pair of horses on the National Mall, with the U.S. Capitol dome in the background, during the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., on June 25. Piovano—Panos Pictures/Redux Yehor Babenko rehearses a production of Eneida with the Veterans’ Theatre in Kyiv on Feb. 18. A Ukrainian border guard, Babenko suffered severe burns to his face, head, and hands; damage to his airways; and the loss of all his fingers during Russian shelling in the Mykolaiv region on March 9, 2022. He now works as a psychologist at the Titanium Rehabilitation Centre and performs with the company. Adapted from Ukrainian writer Ivan Kotliarevsky’s poem, Eneida explores war, memory, and the power of words. The company brings together veterans to draw on their own experiences, with roles adapted to each performer’s physical abilities. —Marylise Vigneau U.S. Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas, right, and the state’s Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa toast with fountain drinks at a Whataburger in Austin on Nov. 3, after an election-night watch party. Talarico, a Democrat, defeated Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the midterms’ most closely watched Senate races. —Brandon Bell—Getty Images Handlers await judgment on their Dalmatians at Crufts, the world’s largest dog show, on March 7. This year some 18,000 dogs were shown across four days in Birmingham, England. Best in Show went to a clumber spaniel named Bruin. —Hannah McKay—Reuters Fans of Marilyn Monroe gather in Palm Springs, Calif., on May 30, two days before what would have been her 100th birthday. Wearing platinum-blond wigs and white dresses inspired by her appearance in The Seven Year Itch (1955), some 1,037 participants set a Guinness World Record for the largest gathering of people dressed as Monroe. —Francesca Forquet—The New York Times/Redux Miss Manhattan Ashley Staggers, in blue, and a young participant in the Empire Stars program wait backstage at the Miss New York pageant in Suffern, N.Y., on June 27. —Tess Mayer Mourners grieve over the body of Mohammad Taha Jafari in Minab, Iran, on March 29. His family had recently learned that his remains had been identified through DNA testing following the Feb. 28 bombing of Shajarat al-Tayyiba Primary School. The attack killed scores of students and teachers on the first day of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. —Hamid Vakili—Anadolu/Getty Images Shelters lie in ruins in Makoko, a fishing community on the Lagos Lagoon in Nigeria, on Jan. 14. Nicknamed the “Venice of Nigeria,” the settlement dates to the 19th century. Lagos state authorities began demolishing homes and evicting residents in late 2025, citing safety concerns near power lines. Residents say the demolitions extended beyond agreed boundaries, leaving families homeless. —Taiwo Aina—The New York Times/Redux Mountaineer Conrad Anker climbs in Canada’s Bugaboo Provincial Park on July 25, photographed by Jimmy Chin on an iPhone 18 Pro. —Jimmy Chin—Courtesy Apple; from the exhibition "What Holds Us" A man takes cover on a highway in Tel Aviv on March 9, during an air raid siren following a missile launch from Iran. —Itai Ron—Haaretz Newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller watches as President Donald Trump speaks to the media upon arriving on Air Force One at Palm Beach International Airport in West Palm Beach, Fla., on Nov. 6. —Tierney L. Cross—The New York Times Mallory Cloud, of Russellville, Ark., votes on a bill concerning Venezuelan oil rights during a Congressional Debate competition at Har-Ber High School in Springdale, Ark., on April 4. Cloud qualified for nationals at the tournament. —Eli Durst—The New Yorker Beachgoers sit at Moutchic beach in Lacanau, southwestern France, as smoke rises from a wildfire on July 24. By then, the blaze in the northern Arcachon Basin had burned more than 3,400 hectares, according to local authorities, and more than 20,000 residents and tourists had been evacuated. The area had also been devastated by wildfires in 2022. —Maximilien Lamy—AFP/Getty Images Volunteers help clear debris at the site of a five-story residential building in Pereira, Colombia, on Aug. 11, a day after it collapsed in a magnitude-7.4 earthquake. items.summary: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system.
